passage: Twenty minutes were left in the maths exam, and the invigilator had stepped out to take a call. Ishita heard paper rustle. Raghav, her best friend since Class 1, had a folded chit under his calculator and was copying formulas. He caught her eye and mouthed, "Please, show me Q7." Her stomach twisted. If she told, he'd be in huge trouble. If she didn't, what about everyone sitting the scholarship test, like Meenal, who had stayed up all week? Ishita shook her head and covered her paper. "Put it away," she whispered. He didn't. After the bell she found him by the stairs. "It's not fair on the others. Tell Sir yourself, or I will." Raghav stared at the floor for a long time. Then he walked slowly toward the staff room, and Ishita went with him.

qa.q: What did Raghav have under his calculator?
qa.a: Raghav had a folded chit under his calculator.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling when Raghav mouthed "Please"?
qa.a: Ishita felt torn: she wanted to protect her best friend but also felt it was unfair on students like Meenal.

qa.q: Which choices by Ishita weighed the harm to others?
qa.a: Refusing to show Q7 and asking Raghav to tell Sir himself protected the fairness of the scholarship test while giving him a chance to own it.

qa.q: How might Raghav see Ishita's "Tell Sir yourself, or I will"?
qa.a: Raghav may feel scared and let down at first, but also that she is giving him the chance to own up.

grounding: Illustrates a child torn between protecting a friend who cheats and fairness, refusing to help and weighing the harm to others.

passage: In the weekly science quiz at their Delhi school, Tejas noticed tiny words inked along Sarika's ruler: "xylem, phloem, stomata." She was his best friend, the one who had shared her tiffin every day since he changed schools. His pencil stopped. At lunch he said, "I saw the ruler." Sarika went pink. "It's just a practice quiz! Don't tell." Tejas thought hard. Nobody else's marks depended on it, but the half-yearly exam was next month. "I won't tell this time. But I'm not covering for you in the real exam, and I won't pass you answers either. Wash it off?" Sarika hesitated, then rubbed the ruler with her thumb until the ink smudged.

qa.q: What words were inked along Sarika's ruler?
qa.a: The words were "xylem, phloem, stomata."

qa.q: Why did Tejas's pencil stop when he saw the ruler?
qa.a: Tejas felt torn and uneasy, caught between loyalty to his best friend and knowing that copying is unfair.

qa.q: How did Tejas weigh the harm before deciding?
qa.a: Since nobody else's marks depended on the practice quiz, he chose to urge Sarika to stop and set a clear limit for the real exam.

qa.q: How does Sarika see Tejas's warning?
qa.a: Sarika is embarrassed and a bit scared, but seems to take it seriously, since she rubs off the ink.

grounding: Shows a child weighing loyalty against honesty after seeing a friend cheat, urging her to stop and refusing to help.

passage: I'm Lavanya, and last month I sat the district maths olympiad in a hall full of kids from other schools. The boy beside me, Darshan by his name card, kept sliding a phone out of his sock and typing. My face got hot. We had all practised for months, and he was just searching for answers! I didn't say anything in the hall. Afterwards I told the invigilator quietly, and she checked the camera footage. The next week, though, I reported a girl in my class for whispering "sorry" when she dropped her pencil. Amma laughed kindly and said, "Big unfairness, yes. Tiny things, let go." I'm still learning where that line is.

qa.q: Where did Darshan keep the phone?
qa.a: Darshan kept sliding a phone out of his sock.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling when Darshan kept typing?
qa.a: Lavanya felt angry and indignant, because everyone had practised for months and he was just searching for answers.

qa.q: What guidance from Amma helps Lavanya with small things?
qa.a: Amma's rule, report big unfairness but let tiny things go, helps Lavanya avoid reporting harmless slips like a whispered sorry.

qa.q: How might Darshan see the invigilator checking the footage?
qa.a: Darshan would likely feel caught and worried, realising someone had noticed the phone.

grounding: Illustrates a child angry at a stranger's cheating who reports it safely, then needs guidance not to report small things.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Friday (Rajni, school counsellor)
Urmila, Class 5, came to me upset after the inter-school general knowledge test in our hall. She saw a student from another school reading answers off his palm. She told the invigilator after the paper, which was the safe, right way, and it was handled. But since then she has reported classmates for sharing a sharpener and for humming during silent reading. Today she said, "Rules are rules!" with clenched fists. I told her I was proud she spoke up about real cheating, and then we sorted examples together: "harms others" versus "small and harmless." I will check in with her next week.

qa.q: What was the student from another school reading answers off?
qa.a: He was reading answers off his palm.

qa.q: What does Urmila's "Rules are rules!" with clenched fists suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Urmila feels strong anger at unfairness, now aimed even at small, harmless things.

qa.q: How did Rajni guide Urmila?
qa.a: Rajni praised the real report, then sorted examples with Urmila into "harms others" and "small and harmless", with a check-in planned.

qa.q: How might the student from the other school see being caught?
qa.a: He may feel embarrassed and afraid, perhaps without knowing who noticed.

grounding: Shows a child's anger at a stranger's cheating leading to a safe report, and a counsellor's guidance against over-reporting small things.

passage: In the school dining hall, Uday made circles with his fingers around his eyes. "Owl girl! Can you even see your roti?" His friends hooted. Sudha's cheeks burned. For a week she ate in the library corridor and stopped raising her hand in class so nobody would look at her. On Friday the counsellor, Mrs Das, sat beside her in the corridor, and they practised a line together. On Monday Uday did the owl eyes again. Sudha looked straight at him. "Yes, they're glasses. They help me see." Then she picked up her tray and walked to Mrs Das's table, where two girls from her class made room.

qa.q: What did Uday call Sudha?
qa.a: Uday called Sudha "Owl girl!"

qa.q: Why did Sudha eat in the library corridor for a week?
qa.a: Sudha felt ashamed and hurt after the teasing and wanted to hide where nobody would look at her.

qa.q: What made Sudha's Monday response work?
qa.a: She answered calmly in a few words, walked away instead of fighting, and went to a supportive adult and classmates.

qa.q: How might Uday see Sudha's calm answer?
qa.a: Uday may feel surprised and a bit foolish, since the joke didn't get the reaction he expected.

grounding: Illustrates a child withdrawing in shame after teasing, then answering calmly, walking away and seeking support.

passage: I'm Jahnavi from the floor above Rekha's. Every evening the colony kids play badminton, and last week they started calling Rekha "Patch-Patch" because her uniform skirt has a darned hole. She stopped coming down. I'd see her at the window, watching. Then on Sunday she came down anyway. When Bunty started the chant, she said, "It's my sister's old skirt. It works fine," in a flat, calm voice, and walked over to the bench where her Mami was sitting. They talked for a while. Then her Mami went and spoke to Bunty's mother. I don't know how Rekha felt inside, but she played the next evening.

qa.q: What did the colony kids call Rekha?
qa.a: They called Rekha "Patch-Patch."

qa.q: What might Rekha have felt while watching from the window?
qa.a: Rekha probably felt hurt and ashamed about the teasing, and lonely watching the game, though Jahnavi can't know for sure.

qa.q: Which steps helped Rekha return to the game?
qa.a: She answered calmly, walked away from Bunty, and went to her Mami for support, who then spoke to Bunty's mother.

qa.q: How might Bunty see Rekha's flat, calm reply?
qa.a: Bunty may be thrown off, since a calm answer takes the fun out of teasing.

grounding: Shows, through a neighbour's eyes, a child withdrawing after teasing and then replying calmly, walking away and getting adult support.

passage:
Monday: Nitin knocked Yash's lunch box into the drain again and laughed. In maths, Yash pressed his pen so hard it tore the page. I hate him, he thought. I wish something terrible would happen to him.
Wednesday: Yash stood behind Nitin in the lunch line, fists tight, imagining shoving him into the tray stack. His heart pounded. He stepped out of line instead and went to find Mr Bose, the class teacher. "Sir, Nitin keeps throwing my lunch in the drain. I'm so angry I want to hurt him." Mr Bose took him into the empty staff room. "Thank you for telling me. Being that angry makes sense. I'll speak to Nitin and his parents today."
Friday: Nitin walked past without a word. Yash's fists stayed open.

qa.q: Where did Nitin knock Yash's lunch box?
qa.a: Nitin knocked Yash's lunch box into the drain.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling in the lunch line on Wednesday?
qa.a: Yash felt furious and full of hatred, imagining hurting Nitin, with his heart pounding.

qa.q: Which choice by Yash was the healthy one, and why?
qa.a: He stepped out of line and told Mr Bose, naming his anger honestly, so an adult could stop the bullying without Yash hitting back.

qa.q: How might Nitin see things after Mr Bose speaks to him and his parents?
qa.a: Nitin may feel caught and embarrassed, and realise his bullying has real consequences.

grounding: Illustrates a bullied child who wants revenge, then admits the anger to a teacher and does not retaliate.

passage: Aadhya, you asked why I rang your teacher that same evening last month, when you told me about Tanvi. Let me tell you about my own school in Aligarh. When I was eleven, a girl called Rukhsana made up a song about my crooked teeth, and the whole class sang it. I lay awake planning revenge: tear her notebook, hide her shoes, make her cry in front of everyone. One morning I stood behind her in the line with my fists clenched, shaking. Then I turned round and went to Miss Fernandez instead. "I'm angry enough to hurt her," I said. She told me the anger was allowed but hurting wasn't, and she stopped the song that very day. That is why your Nani Hafsa picked up the phone.

qa.q: What did Rukhsana make up about Hafsa?
qa.a: Rukhsana made up a song about Hafsa's crooked teeth.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling while standing behind Rukhsana with clenched fists?
qa.a: Hafsa felt furious and humiliated, full of the urge for revenge after the whole class sang the song.

qa.q: Which choice in the story changed things, and why?
qa.a: Turning round and telling Miss Fernandez about the anger, instead of acting on it, let an adult stop the song that same day.

qa.q: How might Miss Fernandez have seen Hafsa's words "I'm angry enough to hurt her"?
qa.a: Miss Fernandez likely took them as honest and brave, and as a sign that the teasing had to stop at once.

grounding: Shows, in a grandmother's memory, a bullied child imagining revenge, then naming the anger to a teacher instead of retaliating.

passage: The school bus had broken down in the rain, and twenty children were waiting in the porch of a closed shop in Aizawl. Lalremsiami, who had snatched Minakshi's pencil box every day for a month, stood apart with a phone to her ear. "Pa, please don't go. Mum is crying." Her voice cracked. Minakshi pretended not to listen, but her anger wobbled. When the replacement bus came, Lalremsiami grabbed the pencil box again. Minakshi held on. "I'm sorry things are hard at home. But you still can't take my things. Give it back." Lalremsiami stared, then let go. The next morning Minakshi told Miss Zote about the snatching. Miss Zote thanked her, spoke to Lalremsiami that day, and asked the counsellor to check in with her too.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami say on the phone?
qa.a: Lalremsiami said, "Pa, please don't go. Mum is crying."

qa.q: Why did Minakshi's anger wobble in the shop porch?
qa.a: Hearing the call, Minakshi felt sympathy and sensed that Lalremsiami might be hurting at home.

qa.q: How did Minakshi balance understanding with a boundary?
qa.a: She said she was sorry things were hard but still refused to let the box go, and told Miss Zote about the snatching.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami see Minakshi's words about home?
qa.a: Lalremsiami may feel exposed and surprised that Minakshi knew, but also seen, which may be why she let go.

grounding: Illustrates a child realising a bully may be hurting at home while still holding a boundary and telling a teacher.

passage: Madhav had called Kiran "Tubelight" all term, loud enough for the whole Class 6 corridor of their Mumbai school to hear. Then on Saturday, at the vegetable market, Kiran saw him carrying heavy bags behind his mother, who was counting coins at every stall. At home Kiran's mother said quietly that Madhav's father had lost his job and the family had moved to a one-room flat. Kiran lay awake. Maybe Madhav was angry about everything. On Monday Madhav started again: "Oi, Tubelight!" Kiran felt a flash of pity, then made a decision. "Madhav, I get that stuff might be hard. Still, don't call me that." When he did it again at lunch, Kiran told Ms Pereira, who spoke to Madhav that afternoon.

qa.q: What had Madhav called Kiran all term?
qa.a: Madhav had called Kiran "Tubelight."

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling on Monday when Madhav started again?
qa.a: Kiran felt a flash of pity for Madhav, along with hurt and a firm wish not to be called names.

qa.q: Why was telling Ms Pereira still right, even after Kiran understood Madhav?
qa.a: Understanding Madhav's troubles explains his behaviour but doesn't excuse it, so the name-calling still needed an adult to stop it.

qa.q: How might Madhav see Kiran's calm "Still, don't call me that"?
qa.a: Madhav might feel surprised, maybe a little ashamed, that Kiran spoke calmly instead of fighting back.

grounding: Shows a child understanding that a bully's hard home life explains his behaviour without excusing it, and keeping a boundary.

passage: Gargi, you and your brother were fighting over the tablet again, so let your Dida Bidisha tell you something. When I was nine, my brother Tapan and I fought about everything: the window seat, the last rasgulla, who Ma loved best. Once we didn't speak for three days over a comic. But one evening at the para football ground, the bigger boys started calling Tapan "Scarecrow" and pulled his shirt. I ran over, stood in front of him and said, "Leave my brother alone or I'm calling Ma." They left. Walking home, Tapan said, "You still owe me that comic." I laughed so hard. We fought all our lives, and we stood up for each other all our lives too.

qa.q: What did the bigger boys call Tapan?
qa.a: They called Tapan "Scarecrow."

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling when she ran to stand in front of Tapan?
qa.a: Bidisha felt protective and angry at the bigger boys, even though she and Tapan fought at home.

qa.q: Which choice in the story showed loyalty, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Standing in front of Tapan and threatening to call Ma showed that home fights didn't stop her defending him outside.

qa.q: How might Tapan have felt when he said "You still owe me that comic"?
qa.a: Tapan probably felt grateful and relieved, and joked to show things were normal between them again 🙂

grounding: Illustrates siblings who fight over things at home yet defend each other outside, so conflict and loyalty coexist.

passage: There was one umbrella and a monsoon downpour, and Ganga and her brother Ojas fought over it all the way down the stairs. "I have a test!" "I'm younger!" She won, and Ojas walked to the bus stop getting soaked, sulking. At the school gate, two Class 8 boys pointed at his dripping hair. "Look, a wet rat!" Ojas's lip trembled. Ganga turned back at once, held the umbrella over him and faced them. "He's my brother. Go find your own joke." They wandered off. Ojas glared at her. "You still took the umbrella." "And you still owe me a chocolate from last week," she said, and shared the umbrella the rest of the way in.

qa.q: What did the Class 8 boys call Ojas?
qa.a: They called Ojas "a wet rat."

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling when she turned back at the school gate?
qa.a: Ganga felt protective and angry at the older boys, even though she had just fought Ojas over the umbrella.

qa.q: What does Ganga's choice at the gate show about sibling conflict?
qa.a: Ganga could fight Ojas over the umbrella yet defend him instantly outside, showing that conflict at home doesn't cancel loyalty.

qa.q: How does Ojas see his sister standing up to the older boys?
qa.a: Ojas probably feels protected and less humiliated, even while still grumbling about the umbrella.

grounding: Shows siblings squabbling over an umbrella in the rain while the older one defends the younger from teasing outside.

passage:
Ganesh Chaturthi, night
Diary, today we brought Bappa home! Aaji told me the story again, about how Ganesha got his elephant head, while Baba fixed the lights. At the evening aarti everyone in our building crowded into the hall, and the dhol was so loud I felt it in my chest. When Aaji put the plate of flames in my hands, I was scared I'd drop it, but my hands went round and round like hers. Everyone was singing "Sukhakarta Dukhaharta." Maria from 4B clapped along too. I don't know why, but my eyes got wet. It felt like the whole building was one family.
Nitin

qa.q: What story did Aaji tell again?
qa.a: Aaji told the story about how Ganesha got his elephant head.

qa.q: Why did Nitin's eyes get wet during the aarti?
qa.a: Nitin felt awe and a deep sense of belonging, with the singing and the dhol making the whole building feel like one family.

qa.q: How could Aaji keep Nitin's wonder growing?
qa.a: Keep sharing stories and small roles like holding the aarti plate, and answer Nitin's questions as they come.

qa.q: How might Maria from 4B experience the aarti?
qa.a: Maria may feel welcomed and curious, joining in the clapping even if the ritual is new to her.

grounding: Illustrates a child feeling devotion, wonder and belonging at a festival, absorbing faith through story, music and ritual.

passage: On Eid morning, the courtyard of Nana's house in the kasba was swept clean and spread with mats. Zeenat, in her new green dupatta, stood in the row behind Nana, between Nani and her cousins, while Nana led the prayer. When everyone bowed together, she bowed too, a little late, peeking at the neat line of backs. Something fluttered in her chest, a quiet, big feeling she had no word for. Afterwards Nani told her the story of the first Eid, and Zeenat asked her to tell it twice. At noon their neighbour Gurleen came over with a box of pinnis, and Zeenat carried back a bowl of sheer khurma, humming the takbir under her breath.

qa.q: What did Gurleen bring at noon?
qa.a: Gurleen came over with a box of pinnis.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling when everyone bowed together?
qa.a: Zeenat felt awe and belonging, a big, quiet feeling fluttering in her chest that she had no word for yet.

qa.q: What helps a child like Zeenat grow in her faith at this age?
qa.a: Joining the family prayer, hearing Nani's stories and humming the takbir let faith grow through ritual and music before any arguments.

qa.q: How might Nani see Zeenat asking for the story twice?
qa.a: Nani likely feels delighted and warm, happy to pass the story on.

grounding: Shows a child feeling wonder and belonging during a family Eid prayer, taking in faith through ritual, story and song.

passage: I'm Neelam, Trisha's cousin, and I share her room. The night before her maths exam, I heard her whisper to the little Krishna on our shelf: "If I get ninety, I'll give up chocolate for a whole month. Promise." She even touched the idol's feet twice, to be sure. The result came: seventy-eight. She sulked and said God hadn't kept the deal. But a week later I heard her whispering again, differently. "Thank you for Priya helping me with fractions. And for Papa not shouting." I don't know what changed in her head. She's still eating chocolate, though.

qa.q: What did Trisha promise to give up?
qa.a: Trisha promised to give up chocolate for a whole month.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling when she said God hadn't kept the deal?
qa.a: Trisha felt disappointed and a bit cheated, since she saw her prayer as a bargain that should have worked.

qa.q: How could an adult gently help Trisha's faith grow?
qa.a: An adult could accept the bargaining as normal and, as Trisha begins to, encourage thank-you prayers for help she already has.

qa.q: How might Neelam see the change in Trisha's prayers?
qa.a: Neelam notices the shift from deals to thanks and is curious, though unsure what changed inside Trisha.

grounding: Illustrates a child bargaining with God for exam marks and beginning to move toward gratitude.

passage:
Sunday: In the church in Aizawl, Lalremsiami squeezed her eyes shut during the prayers. "Lord, if I pass science, I'll sing in the choir every week and never skip Sunday school." She peeked to see if anyone had heard.
Thursday: Science results. Sixty-one, a pass. She hugged her friend Ishita, who had drilled her on the parts of a flower all week. "God kept the deal!" she laughed.
The next Sunday: She stood in the choir as promised. During the silent prayer she didn't ask for anything. She just thought of Ishita's flower drawings and her mother's late-night cocoa, and whispered, "Thank you."

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami promise if she passed science?
qa.a: She promised to sing in the choir every week and never skip Sunday school.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling during the silent prayer the next Sunday?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt grateful rather than hopeful for a deal, thinking of Ishita's help and her mother's cocoa.

qa.q: What does the change across the week suggest for adults who notice bargaining prayers?
qa.a: Bargaining is normal at this age, and gratitude can grow naturally when a child notices the people who helped.

qa.q: How might Ishita see Lalremsiami saying "God kept the deal"?
qa.a: Ishita may be amused, and perhaps a little proud of the flower drills that helped.

grounding: Shows a child's prayer moving over a week from a bargain for marks to simple thanks.

passage:
Monday: Dhruv told Chinmay his family was keeping Paryushan, and that on the last day everyone asks forgiveness. A classmate sniggered, "Jain rules are so weird." Chinmay laughed along, then felt uneasy.
Saturday: Dhruv invited him to the Jain temple near their Ahmedabad pol. Chinmay took off his shoes, kept quiet, and whispered questions. "Why does your family eat before sunset?" "So fewer tiny creatures are harmed," Dhruv's Dada explained, and told him that on the last day people say "Michhami Dukkadam", forgive me if I hurt you.
Sunday: Dhruv folded his hands. "Michhami Dukkadam, Chinmay." Chinmay folded his too. Next day, when the classmate said "weird" again, Chinmay said, "It's not weird. Ask Dhruv. He'll explain."

qa.q: What did Dhruv's Dada say Michhami Dukkadam means?
qa.a: It means forgive me if I hurt you.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay feel uneasy after laughing along?
qa.a: Chinmay felt uneasy and a little guilty, sensing the "weird" comment was unfair to his friend's faith.

qa.q: What did Chinmay do that shows curiosity and respect?
qa.a: He took off his shoes, kept quiet in the temple, asked questions, and later answered the classmate instead of laughing along.

qa.q: How might Dhruv see Chinmay folding his hands?
qa.a: Dhruv likely feels respected and happy that his friend joined the forgiveness ritual 🙏

grounding: Illustrates a child attending a friend's festival of another faith, asking questions and respecting it, and pushing back on mockery.

passage: Tushar, you asked why I bake a plum cake every December. When I was ten, my friend Annamma invited me for Christmas. My aunt muttered, "Why go to their church?" but Amma let me. At midnight the church in our town glowed with candles, and everyone sang songs I didn't know. I kept my hands folded and watched. Afterwards I asked Annamma's mother so many questions: why a baby in a cowshed, why a star, why a cake full of fruit. She answered every one, laughing, and packed a slice for my Amma. My aunt never went into that house. I went every year, and learned that asking is how you stop being afraid of people. So, Tushar, your Paati Nirmala says this year you come with me.

qa.q: What did Annamma's mother pack for Nirmala's Amma?
qa.a: Annamma's mother packed a slice of cake for Nirmala's Amma.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling at the candlelit midnight service?
qa.a: Nirmala felt curious and full of wonder, watching quietly with folded hands among songs she didn't know.

qa.q: Which choice in the story made the difference, and why?
qa.a: Asking Annamma's mother questions instead of staying away like the aunt turned strangeness into understanding and a lifelong friendship.

qa.q: How might Annamma's mother have felt answering all the questions?
qa.a: She likely felt pleased and respected that a guest from another faith cared to understand, which is why she answered laughing.

grounding: Shows, in a grandmother's memory, a child attending a friend's festival, asking questions and respecting rituals unlike her own.

passage: I'm Farhan, and last Diwali I got separated from Abbu at the big fair in Lucknow, with my little cousin Eshaan holding my hand. For a second my legs went wobbly, and Eshaan started crying. Then I remembered what Ammi made us practise: stand still, find a uniform or a shopkeeper, say the number. I saw the police help booth with a loudspeaker, walked straight to it and told the lady constable, "We're lost." Then I said Abbu's number twice, slowly, the way we practised at home. She rang him and announced our names. Ten minutes later Abbu came running, sweaty and laughing, and hugged us both. Eshaan says I was brave. Honestly, I was scared. I just did the steps.

qa.q: Where did Farhan take Eshaan when they were lost?
qa.a: Farhan walked straight to the police help booth.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling right after getting separated from Abbu?
qa.a: Farhan felt scared for a moment, but remembering Ammi's practised steps helped Farhan stay calm.

qa.q: Which steps worked, and why?
qa.a: Standing still, going to a safe person in uniform and saying Abbu's number twice, slowly, let the constable reach him quickly.

qa.q: How might Abbu have felt running to the booth?
qa.a: Abbu probably felt frightened while searching, then hugely relieved, which is why he was sweaty and laughing.

grounding: Illustrates a child who gets lost staying calm, going to a safe person in uniform and repeating the parent's number.

passage:
Trip report, Class 4 zoo visit, Darjeeling (Varun, class teacher)
At 11:40 our head count came up one short: Pema was missing near the red panda enclosure. Before we had finished searching, the zoo ticket office called us. Pema had noticed the group was gone, stood still for a minute, then walked to the ticket counter, told the staff her name and school, and repeated her mother's number and my name clearly. She was calm and dry-eyed when I arrived, though her hands were shaking. I told her she had done exactly the right thing and phoned her mother at once.
Next trip: every child gets a card with the teacher's number, and we will practise the steps as a class.

qa.q: Where was Pema missing?
qa.a: Pema was missing near the red panda enclosure.

qa.q: What do Pema's shaking hands suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: They suggest Pema was frightened inside, even though she stayed calm and dry-eyed enough to follow the steps.

qa.q: What will Varun change for the next trip, and why?
qa.a: Every child will get a card with the teacher's number and the class will practise, so all children can do what Pema did.

qa.q: How might Pema's mother feel getting the phone call?
qa.a: Pema's mother would likely feel a jolt of fear, then relief and pride that Pema knew the number and stayed safe.

grounding: Shows a child who gets separated on a trip staying calm, going to a safe person and repeating the parent's number.
